positive: Weak, diffuse. Fires at the end of a definitional/explanatory noun phrase or clause, especially in math-reasoning text that interprets word-problem wording (e.g. 'a semester is a [block] of time', 'refers to the amount remaining from the previous step[.]', 'means ... 2 hours[,]', '*per semester[*]'); also head nouns completing a parenthetical gloss in Wikipedia ('spore-bearing [cells]'). Typical tokens: the head noun, closing period/comma or markdown asterisk right after a quoted phrase gets explained.
negative: Weak. Function words / pronouns in the middle of a clause right after a subject or modifier: pronoun after an emphasis asterisk ('*[she] received'), 'not' after 'did', verb 'are' after a plural noun, 'children' after 'American Indian', '.S' in 'U.S'. Mid-phrase tokens where the phrase is not yet complete.

positive: Tokens that complete a named entity or a quoted number inside a restated word problem: the final digit of a dollar amount or arithmetic result ('$0.8[5]', '8[0]$'), a noun completing the setup phrase of a quoted problem ('a garden with [vegetables]'), surname pieces in lists of person names ('George [Wyn]yard'). Mostly math-reasoning text quoting the problem statement, plus name lists.
negative: Punctuation closing a coordinate or parenthetical inside code/markup or non-English transliterations: '),' after numeric coordinates in Asymptote label commands like (2-0.05,0.1),W); comma after romanized Chinese titles before Chinese characters; ' in' after a number in Wikipedia dates/figures ('100 in early 2008'). Structural separators after numeric tuples.

positive: Late-layer, Wikipedia science/encyclopedic prose: function words or connectors that open a predicate or complement after a noun/verb, e.g. 'ability [to]', 'synthesis of the [natural]', 'have [been] mined', 'live [and] studio', '[cannot] be ruled out'. Generic continuation tokens in descriptive science/biography text where the next word is a content verb or noun.
negative: Strongly negative inside dense organic-chemistry/technical mechanism prose (e.g. Nazarov cyclization article): subword continuations of technical terms ('undergo[es]', 'conrot[atory]', 'electroc[yclic]') and prepositions in causal technical phrases ('due [to] allylic strain', 'removal [of] β-'). Highly specialized jargon-heavy chemistry sentences.

positive: Comma token (' ,' in tokenized Wikipedia style with space) that ends a noun phrase/clause and is followed by an appositive, a further list item, or a participial/location continuation, NOT by a conjunction: 'subject to interpretation [,] and at any', 'Washington Crossing Bridge [,] which continues', 'for the weekend [,] behind', 'penetrate society [,] politics and business', 'Route 29 [,] just to the'. Commas after a noun ending a phrase, mid-sentence.
negative: Coordinating conjunctions ' and' / ' but' that immediately follow a comma and start a new independent clause in narrative Wikipedia text (', and in one such', ', and over a span', ', but not enough', ', but won only three'). Clause-joining conjunction after comma.

positive: Weak. Odd subword/abbreviation tokens and fixed-phrase completions: 'O[mit]Format' in Asymptote code, 'NR[HP]' (National Register of Historic Places), 'came into [being]', '-[colored]'. Mid-word pieces of acronyms/code identifiers.
negative: Very strong on words of destruction/annihilation: 'destroy', 'Destroy', 'destroyed', 'destruction', 'annihil[ated]', likely also 'decimate', 'demolish', 'wipe out'. Fires on the destruction-verb/noun token (or its suffix piece) in any context, military, astronomical, or political.

positive: Middle subword pieces of rare proper names or uncommon words split into multiple tokens: 'T[umm]ala', 'str[ag]glers', 'Mack[in]ac', 'Ts[uk]uyomi'. The second token of a multi-token name/word, mostly capitalized proper nouns.
negative: The preposition ' for' following an adjective/noun of difficulty, need, or appropriateness that takes a 'for X' complement: 'hard [for]', 'impossible [for]', 'difficult [for]', 'the need [for]', 'in order [for]'. Specifically 'for' introducing who is affected/the beneficiary after evaluative predicates.

positive: Word-initial capital 'T' / lowercase 't' / 'h' token that is the first piece of a word split into a single letter plus remainder: ' T' in 'T-54' / 'T. Rex', ' h'+'atching', ' t'+'ides', ' T'+'iptans'. Single-letter start-of-word tokens in Wikipedia prose.
negative:
Very strong on newline tokens in markdown-structured math reasoning, especially the newline after a heading, label, or line ending with a colon or period that is followed by an indented bullet ('*Calculation:*
    *', '**Big Boxes:**
        *', 'directly.
    *'). Line breaks preceding nested '*' bullets in step-by-step solutions.

positive: Video-game (esp. Sonic the Hedgehog) Wikipedia gameplay description: tokens describing game mechanics such as lives, power-ups, player, checkpoint, completing the game ('three lives ( [power]', 'the [player] continues', 'at any point [in] the game', 'required [to] complete the game'). Also sometimes review-site names in reception sections ('Zap[2]it').
negative: Also video-game articles, but on tokens in development/release/feature-list text: 'unlock[able]', 'occasional [challenging]', and the article ' a' introducing an added feature or mode ('[a] time attack mode', 'add [a] two-player', 'for [a] last encounter'). Articles/adjectives before game features or modes.

positive: Weak. Verbs/prepositions describing range, composition, or source in descriptive prose: 'extends [from]', 'precipitation [falls]', 'prompt [mixes]', 'supported [by]', 'a mix [of]'. Relational connectors that link a subject to its makeup/extent.
negative: In math-reasoning self-checks, the token after 'asks'/'asking' or a quoted phrase that introduces what the problem wants: 'the problem asks [for]', 'is the problem asking [for]', '"..." usually [implies]', '"...?" [implies]'. Meta-reasoning about interpreting the problem's request.

positive: Math-reasoning LaTeX in bullet calculations: the operator or LaTeX command token right after a number or '=' in an inline equation, e.g. '516 \[times]', '3[ \]times', 'B or C[ =]', '=[ $\]frac'. Tokens that start the multiplication/fraction operator in a computation line.
negative: Very strong on spelled-out number words starting a fraction or quantity in prose, especially 'one' in 'one-fourth', 'one-half', 'One-third' after a comma or colon in word problems listing proportions; also '(' before a fraction gloss ('25% [(]quarter)') and 'about [one] mile' in Wikipedia. Words beginning a fractional/proportion phrase.
